description: Periodic table — modern table layout, blocks (s, p, d, f), groups, periods, Mendeleev's contributions, atomic numbers vs masses.

questions.stem: The MODERN PERIODIC TABLE arranges elements in increasing order of:
questions.explanation: MODERN PERIODIC TABLE is arranged in increasing ATOMIC NUMBER (Z = number of PROTONS in nucleus). Established by HENRY MOSELEY (1913) using X-RAY SPECTRA — confirmed atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental ordering principle. CONTRAST WITH MENDELEEV (1869): Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev's first periodic table arranged elements by ATOMIC MASS (with some adjustments). His genius: LEFT GAPS for undiscovered elements (e.g., gallium, germanium); PREDICTED their properties — later confirmed. KEY FACTS: (1) DMITRI MENDELEEV (1834-1907) — 'Father of Periodic Table'; published 1869. (2) HENRY MOSELEY (1887-1915) — discovered atomic number ordering; killed in WWI at Gallipoli, age 27. (3) MODERN PERIODIC LAW: 'Properties of elements are PERIODIC FUNCTIONS of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.' STRUCTURE: 7 PERIODS (rows), 18 GROUPS (columns); 4 BLOCKS (s, p, d, f). KEY PERIODIC TRENDS (memorize for SSC, JEE-Main, NEET): (1) ATOMIC RADIUS — increases DOWN, decreases ACROSS. (2) IONIZATION ENERGY — decreases DOWN, increases ACROSS. (3) ELECTRONEGATIVITY — decreases DOWN, increases ACROSS (peaks at F = 4.0). (4) METALLIC CHARACTER — increases DOWN, decreases ACROSS. (5) ELECTRON AFFINITY — generally increases ACROSS (with exceptions). PYQ FREQUENCY: modern periodic table basis in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: How many GROUPS are there in the MODERN periodic table?
questions.explanation: MODERN PERIODIC TABLE: 18 GROUPS (vertical columns) + 7 PERIODS (horizontal rows). CONTRAST: MENDELEEV's original had 8 groups (Roman I-VIII); modern numbers 1-18 (IUPAC convention since 1988). KEY GROUPS (memorize): (1) GROUP 1 — Alkali Metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) + H. (2) GROUP 2 — Alkaline Earth Metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra). (3) GROUPS 3-12 — d-block / TRANSITION METALS (Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn — Period 4). (4) GROUP 13 — Boron group (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl). (5) GROUP 14 — Carbon group (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb). (6) GROUP 15 — Nitrogen group / pnictogens (N, P, As, Sb, Bi). (7) GROUP 16 — Oxygen group / chalcogens (O, S, Se, Te, Po). (8) GROUP 17 — HALOGENS (F, Cl, Br, I, At). (9) GROUP 18 — NOBLE GASES (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). LANTHANIDES + ACTINIDES — f-block elements; placed below main table for compact layout. NUMBER of ELEMENTS: 118 confirmed (as of 2024). LATEST: Tennessine (117, 2010), Oganesson (118, 2002 — most recent named, 2016). KEY MEMORIZATION: 'Atomic numbers of common elements: H=1, He=2, C=6, N=7, O=8, Na=11, Mg=12, Al=13, Si=14, P=15, S=16, Cl=17, K=19, Ca=20, Fe=26, Cu=29, Zn=30, Ag=47, Au=79, U=92.' UPSC angle: PERIODIC TABLE in NEET + science-tech awareness. PYQ FREQUENCY: groups + periods count in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

questions.explanation: LANTHANIDES (also written 'lanthanoids') — series of 15 elements from LANTHANUM (La, Z=57) to LUTETIUM (Lu, Z=71). Plus YTTRIUM (Y, 39) + SCANDIUM (Sc, 21) commonly grouped → 17 RARE EARTH ELEMENTS (REEs). NAME 'rare earth' is misnomer — they're actually MODERATELY ABUNDANT in Earth's crust (some more than copper) but RARELY found in CONCENTRATED ore deposits. KEY REEs + uses: (1) NEODYMIUM (Nd) — strongest permanent magnets (NdFeB) → wind turbines, EVs, hard drives, headphones. (2) CERIUM (Ce) — catalytic converters, glass polishing. (3) LANTHANUM (La) — camera lenses, batteries (Ni-MH). (4) DYSPROSIUM (Dy) — magnets at high T. (5) EUROPIUM (Eu) — red phosphors in TVs/LEDs. (6) YTTRIUM (Y) — superconductors, lasers. (7) PRASEODYMIUM (Pr) — yellow ceramics. (8) GADOLINIUM (Gd) — MRI contrast agents. WHY SO IMPORTANT: ESSENTIAL for renewable energy (wind, EV magnets), defence (radars, missile guidance), electronics (smartphones), medical imaging. CHINA dominates ~70% of global REE production + ~85% processing. INDIA's REE RESERVES: 6.9 million tonnes (5th largest globally) — mostly in MONAZITE sands (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra coasts). INDIAN RARE EARTHS LIMITED (IREL) — main producer. KEY POLICY: NATIONAL CRITICAL MINERALS LIST released 2023 — 30 critical minerals including most REEs. UPSC angle: STRATEGIC MINERALS + CHINA dependency reduction; India-Australia critical minerals agreement. PYQ FREQUENCY: REEs in UPSC PT, GS-3 economy, current affairs 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: MENDELEEV LEFT GAPS in his periodic table for:
questions.explanation: MENDELEEV (1869) — anticipated existence of UNDISCOVERED elements; left gaps + PREDICTED their properties using PERIODIC TRENDS. PROPHECY CONFIRMED: (1) GALLIUM (Ga, Z=31) — predicted as 'eka-aluminium' (eka = beyond, Sanskrit). Discovered 1875 by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in France. Predicted: atomic mass ~68; actual: 70. (2) GERMANIUM (Ge, Z=32) — predicted as 'eka-silicon'. Discovered 1886 by Winkler in Germany. (3) SCANDIUM (Sc, Z=21) — predicted as 'eka-boron'. Discovered 1879 by Nilson in Sweden. KEY: Mendeleev's PROPERTIES were REMARKABLY ACCURATE — atomic mass, density, oxide formulas, compounds — within ~5%. This was the GREATEST TRIUMPH of his periodic law + earned scientific acceptance. SANSKRIT PREFIXES used by Mendeleev: 'EKA' (one beyond), 'DVI' (two beyond), 'TRI' (three beyond). e.g., 'ekaboron' = next-down from boron in same group. UPSC angle: SCIENCE in INDIA's COLONIAL era; Sanskrit's influence on Western science. ALSO MENDELEEV's PREDICTIONS extended to: (a) Reorder some elements (atomic-mass anomalies — e.g., Te before I despite slightly higher mass, because chemistry suggested otherwise; later confirmed by Moseley using atomic number). (b) Group Re/Tc as homologs, even though Tc was undiscovered. NOBEL: Mendeleev was NOMINATED 5 times — never won (controversial; politics in Nobel committee). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mendeleev's predictions in NEET, NCERT, history-of-science 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which element has the HIGHEST ELECTRONEGATIVITY?
questions.explanation: FLUORINE (F) — most electronegative element. PAULING SCALE: F = 4.0 (highest possible — used as reference). KEY ELECTRONEGATIVITIES: F > O (3.5) > N ≈ Cl (3.0-3.2) > Br (2.96) > I, S (2.5-2.6) > C, H (~2.5, 2.1) > metalsel (Na 0.9, Cs 0.7 lowest). DEFINITION: ELECTRONEGATIVITY = ability of an atom in a molecule to ATTRACT BONDED ELECTRONS. KEY TRENDS: (1) ACROSS A PERIOD: increases (atoms get smaller, nucleus pulls more strongly). (2) DOWN A GROUP: decreases (more inner shielding). PEAK at F (top-right of metals); LOWEST at Cs/Fr (bottom-left). KEY CONSEQUENCES: (1) HIGH-electronegativity-pair → IONIC bond (e.g., NaCl: ENs differ by 2.1). (2) LOW-difference → COVALENT bond (CCl₄). (3) Electronegativity DIFFERENCE PREDICTS BOND POLARITY: Δ > 1.7 = ionic; 0.4-1.7 = polar covalent; < 0.4 = nonpolar covalent. DIPOLE MOMENT in molecules depends on electronegativity differences. WATER (H₂O): Δ_OH = 1.4 → polar; bent shape → permanent dipole; explains H₂O's UNIQUE properties (high BP, surface tension, universal solvent). FLUORINE compounds: HF (hydrofluoric — etches glass), CFCs (banned), Teflon (PTFE — non-stick), fluorides in toothpaste. KEY: FLUORINE the SMALLEST + MOST AGGRESSIVE oxidizer in nature; reacts with EVERYTHING incl. noble gases (XeF₂, XeF₄). UPSC angle: chemical bonding + electronegativity in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Elements in the SAME GROUP of the periodic table have similar:
questions.explanation: ELEMENTS in same GROUP have SAME NUMBER of VALENCE ELECTRONS — explaining their similar chemical behavior. EXAMPLES: (1) GROUP 1 (alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) — all have ONE valence electron; all form +1 ions, react vigorously with water, etc. (2) GROUP 17 (halogens: F, Cl, Br, I) — all have SEVEN valence electrons; all form −1 ions; all need ONE more electron for octet → highly reactive. (3) GROUP 18 (noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) — all have FULL outer shells (8 electrons; He has 2); all are mostly INERT. (4) GROUP 14 (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb) — 4 valence electrons; tend to form 4 covalent bonds. KEY VALENCE PATTERN by group: GROUP 1: 1 outer e⁻; GROUP 2: 2; GROUP 13: 3; GROUP 14: 4; GROUP 15: 5; GROUP 16: 6; GROUP 17: 7; GROUP 18: 8 (or 2 for He). MIDDLE-GROUP (transition metals, Groups 3-12): variable d-electron counts; complex bonding. WITHIN GROUP — TRENDS: as you go DOWN: (1) Atomic radius INCREASES (more shells). (2) Reactivity INCREASES (alkali metals) or DECREASES (halogens). (3) Metallic character INCREASES. (4) Ionization energy DECREASES. (5) Electronegativity DECREASES. PERIOD vs GROUP: PERIOD = number of SHELLS; GROUP = number of OUTER ELECTRONS. Period 4 element: 4 shells. Group 7 (halogens): 7 outer e⁻. UPSC angle: chemistry foundations needed for NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-tested. PYQ FREQUENCY: same-group properties in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which is the HEAVIEST NATURALLY-OCCURRING element?
questions.explanation: URANIUM (U, Z=92) — heaviest NATURALLY-OCCURRING element on Earth in significant quantities (in uraninite/pitchblende ore). Trace amounts of NEPTUNIUM (93) + PLUTONIUM (94) found NATURALLY (from cosmic-ray + uranium-decay processes — extreme trace). ELEMENTS BEYOND URANIUM: 'TRANSURANIUM' — all SYNTHETIC (created in reactors/accelerators). KEY DISCOVERIES of TRANSURANIC elements: (1) Np (1940), Pu (1940-41) — Berkeley Lab. (2) Am, Cm, Bk, Cf — Berkeley, Glenn Seaborg's group. (3) Es, Fm — discovered in fallout from H-bomb tests! (4) Md (101), No (102), Lr (103). (5) RUTHERFORDIUM (104) onwards — heavy-ion collisions. (6) OGANESSON (118) — most recent (2002, named 2016 after YURI OGANESSIAN, Russian physicist; only one ever made). HEAVIEST elements have very SHORT half-lives (microseconds for some); only a few atoms ever produced. URANIUM PROPERTIES: silvery-white metal; very dense (19 g/cm³ — denser than lead). USES: nuclear reactors (U-235), nuclear weapons, depleted uranium (DU) in armor-piercing munitions, ceramics. RADIOACTIVE: U-238 half-life 4.5 BILLION YEARS (~age of Earth!). U-235 half-life 700 million years. NATURAL OCCURRENCE: found in granite, ocean water (~3 ppb), monazite sand. INDIA's URANIUM RESERVES: ~118,000 tonnes (Jharkhand — Jaduguda mine; Andhra — Tummalapalle mine; Meghalaya). HEAVIEST STABLE element: BISMUTH (Z=83) — was thought stable; recently shown to be slightly radioactive (half-life 10²⁰ years — longer than age of universe!). PYQ FREQUENCY: uranium-related in NEET, GA 1× per cycle.
